DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Donald Anderson issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) concluding that Respondent Chicago Transit Authority
(“CTA” or “Employer”) did not engage in unfair labor practices in violation of Section 10(a) of the
Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., as alleged by Charging Party Erek
Slater. On June 20, 2025, Charging Party filed two documents, one titled “Charging Party’s
Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s Recommended Decision and Order” (“Exceptions”), and
the other titled “Charging Party’s Brief in Support of Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s
Recommended Decision and Order” (“Supporting Brief”), challenging the ALJ’s recommendations.
Respondent then filed a Motion to Strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Brief in Support of
Exceptions (“Motion to Strike”), contending that Charging Party’s filings do not comport with the
requirements set by Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules and Regulations (“Board’s Rules”).
Charging Party filed a response to Respondent’s Motion to Strike and filed a Motion for Section
1200.160 Variance of the Rules and Leave to Re-File Combined Exceptions and Brief in Support of
Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument on Exceptions (“Motion for Variance and Leave”).
Respondent filed a timely response to Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave.
1

Respondent’s Motion to Strike
Respondent moves to strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief, contending
that such filings total 89 pages, exceeding the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.40(b) of the
Board’s Rules. The Respondent further asserts that Charging Party’s Exceptions, totaling 61 pages,
is also a “brief” because it contains argument in support of each exception included in that document.
Respondent contends that Charging Party has thus filed two briefs, without leave to do so, which is
not allowed under the Board’s Rules. Respondent also contends that Charging Party filed the 61-
page Exceptions, which exceeds the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.140(b) without leave to
do so. In support, Respondent points to other instances where Charging Party’s filings have skirted
the rules, such as the filings related to Charging Party’s motion to amend the complaint and the filing
of Charging Party’s post-hearing brief. Respondent urges the Board to strike both documents due to
the difficulty in deciding which pages of the documents to strike.
In his response, Charging Party asserts that Section 1200.135(b) and Section 1200.140
contemplate that exceptions are separate documents from briefs in support of exceptions because
Section 1200.140(a)(3) defines “Briefs” in terms of “briefs in support of exceptions” and omits
“exceptions” in that definition. (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 5). Charging Party notes that Section
1200.140(a)(3) defines “briefs in support of exceptions” as “inclusive of any separate exceptions [ .
. .] filed with the brief” and contends that a reasonable reading of that definition is that “Section
1200.143(a)(3) contemplates a ‘brief’ with exceptions separate and additional to the exceptions
already filed in a party’s ‘exceptions’ document and therefore only ‘filed with the brief’ not with the
‘exceptions’.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). Charging Party reasons that “there would be no
need to identify a ‘brief in support of exceptions’ absent ‘exceptions’ that the brief was directed
2

toward supporting.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). Charging Party further states that “the
contemplation of ‘separate exceptions’ that are ‘filed with the brief’ is reasonable in that some
exceptions may not need extensive argument and therefore would not require a party to duplicate an
‘exception’ in an ‘exception’ document and in a brief.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). As such,
Charging Party argues that the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.140(b) applies only to
supporting briefs and does not include a page limit for exceptions when they are filed as a separate
document. Charging Party further asserts that his counsel conducted extensive research and found
no cases on this issue. Charging Party also states that his counsel consulted other attorneys who have
filed separate exceptions and contends that they have filed exceptions in addition to a supporting
brief which, when combined, totaled more than 50 pages.
Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave to Re-File
Charging Party seeks a variance from the Board’s Rules that govern filing deadlines for
exceptions and page limits for briefs and requests leave to re-file its exceptions and brief as a single
document not exceeding 60 pages. Charging Party contends all three criteria for granting variances
are satisfied: (1) the rules are not statutorily mandated; (2) Respondent would not be prejudiced by
granting a variance as Respondent has already previewed Charging Party’s arguments and can more
readily respond to them; and (3) it would unreasonable and duly burdensome for the Board to strictly
adhere to these rules where the consequences of striking his exceptions would constitute a waiver of
his challenges to the RDO.
Respondent opposes Charging Party’s motion. Respondent contends that Charging Party
“confuses quantity with complexity” and claims that the reason the record contains multiple volumes
of testimony and exhibits can be attributed to Charging Party’s litigation strategy to “muddy
the record.” Respondent asserts that allowing Charging Party to re-file as a single, combined
exceptions and supporting brief document totaling 50 pages would prejudice Respondent because it
3

would then need to seek leave to respond to Charing Party’s over-sized exceptions and supporting
brief with its own over-sized response.
Discussion
Both motions revolve around Sections 1200.135(b) and 1200.140 of the Board’s Rules.
Section 1200.135(b) outlines the process and requirements for the Board’s review of an ALJ’s RDO
and provides in relevant part:
b) Administrative Law Judge's Recommended Decision and Order
1) Proceedings
* * * *
B) In unfair labor practice proceedings, parties may file
exceptions to the Administrative Law Judge’s
recommended decision and order, and briefs in support of
those exceptions, no later than 30 days after service of the
recommended decision and order. . . .
C) In either type of proceeding, exceptions, responses,
cross-exceptions, cross-responses and briefs, shall be filed
with the Board’s General Counsel in the Board's Chicago
office. A party not filing timely exceptions waives its right
to object to the Administrative Law Judge’s recommended
decision and order.
* * * *
2) Exceptions and/or cross-exceptions shall specifically set
forth the questions of procedure, fact, law or policy to
which exception is taken, shall identify that part of the
Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and
order to which objection is made, and shall state the
grounds for the exceptions and shall include the citation of
authorities and citations to the record unless set forth in a
supporting brief. Any exception to a ruling, finding,
conclusion or recommendation that is not specifically
urged shall be deemed to have been waived. Any exception
that fails to comply with the foregoing requirements may
be disregarded.
3) Any brief in support of exceptions shall be confined to the
subjects raised in the exceptions and shall contain:
A) a clear and concise statement of the case containing all
that is material to the consideration of the questions
4

presented;
B) a specification of the questions involved and the issues
to be argued; and
C) an argument, presenting clearly the points of fact and
law relied upon in support of the position taken on each
question.
* * * *
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) and (b)(3) (emphasis added). Section 1200.135(c) provides that
“Parties desiring oral argument before the Board shall request oral argument and state the reasons for
the requests in their appeals, exceptions and responses. . . .” 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(c)
(emphasis added).
Section 1200.140(a) states in relevant part:
a) For purposes of this Section, “briefs” shall be deemed to
include:
* * * *
3) briefs in support of exceptions and cross-exceptions to an
Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and order
and responses to that decision and order, inclusive of any
separate exceptions, cross-exceptions or response document
filed with the brief;
* * * *
b) All briefs, including supporting materials, shall be no more than
a total of 50 double-spaced pages with margins of at least ½
inch, including attachments. All of the pages in excess of the 50
page limit will be rejected, unless leave is granted. In the
extraordinary circumstance that a case involves extremely
complex issues, issues of first impression, or a lengthy factual
record, a party may seek leave to file a brief in excess of 50
pages by filing a motion requesting leave. Motions seeking
leave must be filed before the deadline for filing the brief at
issue and should be directed to the Administrative Law Judge
with whom the brief is pending or the General Counsel if the
brief is on a matter before the Board.
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.140(a) and (b) (emphasis added).
5

For the reasons discussed below, we grant Respondent’s Motion to Strike but also grant
Charging Party’s motion for a variance to re-file its Exceptions and Supporting brief as a single
document comprising 60 pages within five business days of service of the Board’s order.
Although the Board’s Rules recognize that exceptions may be filed as a separate document
and do not set a page limit specifically on “exceptions” per se, Section 1200.140(b) clearly defines
“Briefs” to include “briefs in support of exceptions . . . , inclusive of any separate exceptions, cross-
exceptions or response document filed with the brief.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.140(a)(3) (emphasis
added). And because Section 1200.140(b) limits all briefs, including supporting material to 50 pages,
absent leave to file a brief in excess of that page limit, Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting
Brief do not comport with Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules.1
We are unpersuaded that Charging Party’s interpretation of Section 1200.140(a)(3) is a
reasonable interpretation of the that rule. Charging Party states that “Section 1200.143(a)(3)
contemplates a ‘brief’ with exceptions separate and additional to the exceptions already filed in a
party’s ‘exceptions’ document and therefore only ‘filed with the brief’ not with the ‘exceptions’,”
and reasons that “there would be no need to identify a ‘brief in support of exceptions’ absent
‘exceptions’ that the brief was directed toward supporting.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16)
(emphasis in the original). Essentially, Charging Party interprets Section 1200.140(a)(3) to apply
only when a party elects to file exceptions and then files more exceptions in a supporting brief
because, as Charging Party asserts, “some exceptions may not need extensive argument and therefore
would not require a party to duplicate an ‘exception’ in an ‘exception’ document and in a brief.” (CP
1 On April 28, 2025, Charging Party filed an unopposed motion for a 30-day extension of time, which the Board’s General
Counsel granted, asserting the very same reasons he now claims require a variance from the Board’s Rules. It is unclear
why, and Charging Party offers no further explanation, Charging Party did not also ask for leave to file a brief in excess
of 50 pages or for clarification of the rules.
6

Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16) (emphasis in the original). This interpretation, however, is at odds with
Section 1200.135(b)(2), which allows parties to state the grounds in support of its exceptions in a
“supporting brief” subject to the constraints stated in Section 1200.135(b)(3), chief among them
being the constraint that “Any brief in support of exceptions shall be confined to the subjects raised
in the exceptions.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) and (b)(3) (emphasis added). Because
Section 1200.135(b)(2) immediately precedes Section 1200.135(b)(3), Section 1200.135(b)(3) can
only be read to mean that if a party submits exceptions and elects to justify those exceptions in a
brief, that brief must only discuss those exceptions and cannot assert additional exceptions.
We strike the entirety of both Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief in large
part because we grant Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave to the extent Charging Party
may re-file his exceptions and brief in support as a single document representing “Charging Party’s
Exceptions and Brief in Support of Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument,” as stated in his
motion.
The criteria we use in considering a request for variances are provided in Section 1200.160 of
the Board’s Rules and are as follows:
a) the provision from which the variance is granted is not statutorily mandated;
b) no party will be injured by the granting of the variance; and
c) the rule from which the variance is granted would, in the particular case, be
unreasonable or unnecessarily burdensome.
80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.160. The decision to grant a variance pursuant to the above criteria is made
at our discretion. Wood Dale Fire Prot. Dist. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., State Panel, 395 Ill. App. 3d
523, 530 (2d Dist. 2009) (holding that granting a variance under Board’s rules is left to Board’s
discretion, unless such decision is arbitrary or capricious); see also State of Ill., Dep’t of Cent. Mgmt.
Servs., 25 PERI 31 (IL LRB-SP Gen Counsel Order 2009), rev’d sub nom in State of Ill., Dep’t of
7

Central Mgmt. Servs. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., State Panel, et al., 26 PERI ¶ 77 (4th Dist. Rule 23
Order) (reversed and remanded for consideration of the merits of exceptions).
Applying the above criteria to this case, we find all three criteria satisfied. The 50-page
limitation set forth Section 1200.140.(b) and the 30-day timeframe for filing exceptions to a
recommended decision and order in unfair labor practice proceedings set forth in Section
1200.135(b)(1)(B) are not statutorily mandated; Respondent would not be prejudiced by allowing the
appeal because even if the Board were to allow the late filing, Respondent still would have the
opportunity to respond to the exceptions; and strictly adhering to the timeframe could be construed
as unreasonable and unduly burdensome in this particular case considering that Charging Party did
timely file exceptions, albeit incorrectly, and should not have to suffer the consequence of waiving
Board review of the RDO due to his attorney’s incorrect interpretation of the Board’s Rules.
To address Respondent’s concern regarding the need to seek leave to file a response in excess
of 50 pages, we proactively grant such leave in addition to resetting the due date for Respondent to
respond to Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions and brief in support. In addition, our resetting the
due date to respond to Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions does not change the due date, July 25,
2025, for Charging Party to respond to Respondent’s exceptions.
For the reasons set forth above, we strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief
but grant the requested variance and allow Charging Party to re-file within 5 days of service of the
our Decision and Order its exceptions and brief in support as a single document representing
“Charging Party’s Exceptions and Brief in Support of Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument,”
as stated in his motion, not to exceed 60 pages exclusive of certificate of service. Charging Party’s
filing must otherwise comply with Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules. In addition, we grant
Respondent leave to file its response in excess of 50 pages and such response is due within 15 days
of service of Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions.
